title: The Reformed hold that free choice belongs to the rational creature and was not lost by sin
source_text: II. Sed constans est Reformatorum omnium sententia liberum arbitrium simpliciter consideratum, & secundum propriam naturam atque essentiam, esse aliquid quod a creatura rationali separari non potest: adeoque libere agendi facultatem ab homine per peccatum prorsus sublatam non fuisse: imo hominem per peccatum corruptum non minus libere agere quae agit, quam agebat ante peccatum: ac seu sibi relictus peccato indulgeat, id plane summa cum libertate facere; sive per gratiam motus & excitatus meliori vitae studeat, actus illius quoque liberos esse, neque per gratiae Dei efficaciam quicquam libertati voluntatis ejus praejudicari.
pass_a_gloss: But it is the constant opinion of all the Reformed that free choice considered simply, and according to its proper nature and essence, is something which cannot be separated from a rational creature: and so the faculty of acting freely was not altogether taken away from man through sin: indeed that man corrupted through sin acts no less freely the things he does, than he acted before sin: and whether, left to himself, he indulges sin, he does this plainly with the greatest liberty; or, moved and stirred up by grace, he strives after a better life, his acts also are free, and nothing is prejudiced to the liberty of his will through the efficacy of the grace of God.
pass_b_english: Yet all the Reformed consistently hold that free choice, taken simply and in its own nature and essence, cannot be separated from a rational creature. So sin did not wholly remove man's power to act freely.

Indeed, man corrupted by sin acts no less freely in what he does than he did before sin. If he is left to himself and gives way to sin, he does it with complete freedom. If grace moves and rouses him to pursue a better life, those acts are free too, and the efficacy of God's grace takes nothing away from his will's freedom.

choices.english: takes nothing away from his will's freedom
choices.why: Praejudicare here means to impair or prejudice a right; 'take away from' gives the sense without legal jargon.
